title: Word Relations, Closures, and Equivalence Classes (Wortrelationen, Abschlüsse und Äquivalenzklassen)
summary: This unit examines properties of endorelations (Endorelationen) and classifies important examples as equivalence relations (Äquivalenzrelationen) or partial orders (partielle Ordnungen). It introduces word relations (Wortrelationen) such as prefixes, infixes, and conjugacy (Konjugation), and shows how transitive closures describe reachability (Erreichbarkeit). Equivalence classes group related elements into quotients and partitions.
keyFacts: An endorelation on A is a subset of A×A.
Reflexivity requires aRa for every a; irreflexivity forbids every aRa.
Symmetry requires that bRa also holds whenever aRb holds.
Antisymmetry forbids mutual relations only between distinct elements.
Asymmetry forbids every reverse relation and therefore also self-relations.
An equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.
A partial order is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive.
Congruence modulo a fixed positive m is an equivalence relation on ℤ.
Σᵏ contains all words of length k over Σ; Σ* contains all finite words, including ε.
A prefix occurs at the beginning, a suffix at the end, and an infix is a contiguous part of a word.
Two words are conjugate if one can be transformed into the other by cutting it and then swapping the two parts.
The prefix, suffix, and infix relations are partial orders.
Conjugacy is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.
R⁺ = ⋃ₖ≥1 Rᵏ describes reachability in at least one step.
R* = Id_A ∪ R⁺ also allows paths of length zero and is reflexive-transitive.
An equivalence class [a]ᵣ contains all elements equivalent to a.
A/R is the set of all equivalence classes and forms a partition of A when R is an equivalence relation.
A representative system chooses exactly one element from each equivalence class.

review.notes: Korrigiert: falscher Lösungsschlüssel bei |R*|, eine abweichende Überschriftenangabe und fehlende Definitionen für Kongruenz, Äquivalenzklasse und R⁺ ergänzt. Prüfrechnungen und übrige Antwortmengen stimmen.

questions.prompt: What form does an endorelation on a set $A$ take?
questions.explanation: For an endorelation, both entries of every ordered pair come from the same underlying set A.

questions.prompt: Which statements correctly express the definitions of the relation properties? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Symmetric means: If aRb, then bRa.
Asymmetric means: If aRb, then bRa.
Antisymmetric means: If aRb and bRa, then a=b.
Reflexive means: aRa holds for every a.

questions.explanation: The first three statements give the respective definitions. For asymmetry, aRb must imply that bRa does not hold.

questions.prompt: For an alphabet $\Sigma$, $\Sigma^k$ contains all words with exactly ___ symbols.
questions.explanation: Here, the exponent k denotes the exact word length.

questions.prompt: An antisymmetric relation may contain loops aRa, as long as mutual relations between distinct elements are ruled out.
questions.explanation: Antisymmetry requires that a=b whenever aRb and bRa. A loop satisfies this condition because the two elements are equal.

questions.prompt: Let $\Sigma=\{a,b\}$. What is $\Sigma^0$?
questions.explanation: The empty word ε is the only word of length 0.

questions.prompt: The empty word $\varepsilon$ has length ___.
questions.explanation: ε contains no symbols, so its length is 0.

questions.prompt: Which statements about prefixes, suffixes, and infixes are correct? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: $u$ is a prefix of $v$ if there is a word $w$ such that $uw=v$.
An infix may combine symbols from separate positions in the word.
$u$ is a suffix of $v$ if there is a word $w$ such that $wu=v$.
$u$ is an infix of $v$ if it occurs as a contiguous part of $v$.

questions.explanation: Prefixes occur at the beginning, suffixes at the end, and infixes form a contiguous segment. Symbols scattered across a word do not form an infix.

questions.prompt: $R^+$ collects pairs connected by paths of at least one step; paths of length zero are not included.
questions.explanation: $R^+=\bigcup_{k\ge1}R^k$ starts at k=1. The zero-step path is included only in $R^*$.

questions.prompt: Which path lengths are allowed by the reflexive-transitive closure $R^*$?

options.text: Only positive even numbers of steps

questions.explanation: $R^*=\bigcup_{k\ge0}R^k$ also contains $R^0=\operatorname{Id}_A$, that is, the zero-step paths.

questions.prompt: If $R$ is an equivalence relation on $A$, its equivalence classes form a partition of $A$.
questions.explanation: For an equivalence relation, the classes are nonempty, pairwise disjoint, and together equal the underlying set.

questions.prompt: How should the equality relation on a set be classified?

options.text: It is only a partial order.
It is both an equivalence relation and a partial order.
It is neither an equivalence relation nor a partial order.
It is only an equivalence relation.

questions.explanation: Equality is reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric, and transitive. It therefore satisfies both sets of properties.

questions.prompt: For $\Sigma=\{a,b\}$, how many words does $\Sigma^2$ contain?
questions.explanation: There are two symbol choices for each of the two positions, so there are $2\cdot2=4$ words: aa, ab, ba, and bb.

questions.prompt: For a fixed positive $m=4$, $x\equiv_4 y$ holds exactly when $4$ divides $x-y$. Which statement holds for $7$ modulo $4$?
questions.explanation: $7-3=4$ is a multiple of 4. The other differences are not multiples of 4.

questions.prompt: For $u=bc$ and $v=abcd$, which word relation holds between $u$ and $v$?

options.text: $u$ is an infix of $v$, but neither a prefix nor a suffix.

questions.explanation: In $abcd$, $bc$ occurs contiguously in the middle. There is still an a at the beginning and a d at the end, so it is neither a prefix nor a suffix.

questions.prompt: A word is cut at $ab\cdot cde$; the two parts are then swapped. Which word results?
questions.explanation: At the cut $ab\cdot cde$, the right part is placed before the left: $cdeab$.

questions.prompt: An arrow leads from the source to the destination. Which nodes are reachable from 4 by following at least one arrow?

context.caption: Directed graph; arrows point from source to destination.

questions.explanation: No arrow leaves 4 in the diagram. Therefore, there is no path of positive length from 4.

questions.prompt: On $A=\{p,q\}$, let $R=\{(p,q)\}$. How many pairs does the reflexive-transitive closure $R^*$ contain?
questions.explanation: $R^*$ contains the two identity pairs $(p,p)$ and $(q,q)$, as well as the existing pair $(p,q)$.

questions.prompt: For $m=5$, $14\equiv_5 4$ holds because the difference is an integer multiple of 5.
questions.explanation: $14-4=10=2\cdot5$, so the numbers are congruent modulo 5.
The class of 1 contains exactly the elements related to 1: 1 and 2.

questions.prompt: How many prefixes does the word $abca$ have, counting the empty word and the word itself?
questions.explanation: There is one prefix of each length from 0 to 4: ε, a, ab, abc, and abca.

questions.prompt: Consider the subset relation on the power set $\mathcal P(\{x,y\})$. Which pair satisfies $U\subseteq V$?
questions.explanation: Every element of {x} also belongs to {x,y}; in each other case, at least one element of U is missing from V.

questions.prompt: Which of the following relations are partial orders? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Congruence modulo a fixed positive $m$ on $\mathbb Z$

questions.explanation: Equality, less-than-or-equal-to, and the subset relation are reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive. Strictly less than is not reflexive; congruence modulo m is not antisymmetric.

questions.prompt: On $\mathbb Z$, let divisibility by $a\mid b\iff\exists k\in\mathbb Z: b=ka$ be defined. Which properties hold? More than one answer may be correct.
questions.explanation: For reflexivity, choose k=1; if b=ka and c=ℓb, then c=(ℓk)a. Symmetry and antisymmetry fail, for example, with 2|4 and with 1|-1 as well as -1|1.

questions.prompt: For a relation $R$, $R^+$ is the smallest transitive closure that contains all pairs from $R$.
questions.explanation: $R^+$ adds exactly the relations forced by paths of positive length and contains the original pairs.

questions.prompt: Which property always follows from asymmetry?
questions.explanation: If aRa held, asymmetry would also require ¬(aRa). Therefore, no loop can exist.

questions.prompt: Let $A=\{u,v,w\}$ and $R=\{(u,v),(v,w)\}$. A pair $(x,y)$ belongs to $R^*$ exactly when there is a directed path from $x$ to $y$ with any number of edges; paths with 0 edges also count. How many ordered pairs does $R^*$ contain?
questions.explanation: The three 0-edge paths give $(u,u),(v,v),(w,w)$. Add the two edges in $R$ and the path $u\to v\to w$, which adds $(u,w)$. There are 6 pairs in total.

questions.prompt: The quotient $A/R$ consists of the equivalence classes. How many elements does this quotient have?

  K2 --> R2["Representative: xyz"]
context.caption: Assignment of words to their classes and one representative for each.

questions.explanation: The diagram shows two classes, K₁ and K₂. Each class counts as one element of the quotient.

questions.prompt: A directed graph has $n$ nodes. Which statement explains why a path of at most $n-1$ steps suffices for reachable distinct nodes?

options.text: Every directed graph has at most $n-1$ edges.
Repeated nodes can be removed from a path without losing reachability.
Every path must visit all nodes exactly once.
Self-relations do not count as steps.

questions.explanation: A path without unnecessary cycles does not visit any node more than once. It therefore needs at most n−1 edges between distinct nodes.

source.heading: Warum reichen hier endlich viele Potenzen?

questions.prompt: The reflexive-transitive closure can be written as $R^*= $ ___.
questions.explanation: R* adds all pairs of the identity relation to the transitive closure R⁺, that is, the zero-step paths.

questions.prompt: Which statements about conjugacy are correct? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Conjugate words are obtained by cutting a word and swapping the two parts.
Any permutation of the letters produces a conjugate word.
The cyclic order of the symbols is preserved.

questions.explanation: Conjugacy allows cyclic shifts, not arbitrary permutations. It is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.

questions.prompt: On $A=\{1,2,3\}$, let $R=\{(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(1,2),(2,1)\}$. How many classes are in the partition $A/R$?
questions.explanation: The classes are {1,2} and {3}, so the quotient has two elements.

questions.prompt: The infix relation is transitive: If $u$ is a contiguous part of $v$ and $v$ is a contiguous part of $z$, then $u$ is a contiguous part of $z$.
questions.explanation: If we write $v=puq$ and $z=rvs$, then $z=(rp)u(qs)$. Thus, u remains a contiguous part of z.

source.heading: Warum sind alle drei partielle Ordnungen?

questions.prompt: On $A=\{a,b\}$, let $R=\{(a,b)\}$. The transitive closure $R^+$ contains exactly the pairs connected by at least one R-step. Does $R^+$ contain the pair $(a,a)$?
questions.explanation: The only arrow from a leads to b, and no arrow leads back from b. Therefore, there is no path of positive length from a to a.

questions.prompt: In a directed graph, $R^k$ represents the pairs connected by a path of exactly k edges. How many node entries does a path of length $k$ have?
questions.explanation: A path with k edges has a starting node and one additional node entry after each edge, for a total of k+1 entries.

questions.prompt: In Boolean matrix multiplication for relation composition, a 1 indicates that at least one suitable intermediate node exists; it does not count how many paths there are.
questions.explanation: The composition uses AND to check an intermediate node and combines possible intermediate nodes with OR. Thus, multiple paths still yield a single truth value of 1.

questions.prompt: For words $u=ab$ and $v=baa$, their concatenation is $uv=abbaa$. What is its length?
questions.explanation: Concatenation adds the lengths: $|uv|=|u|+|v|=2+3=5$.

questions.prompt: On $A=\{0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7\}$, let $xRy$ hold exactly when $x\equiv_4 y$, where $x\equiv_4 y$ means that $x-y$ is a multiple of 4. How many equivalence classes does $A/R$ have?
questions.explanation: The elements are grouped according to their remainders 0, 1, 2, and 3 modulo 4, giving four classes.

questions.prompt: How many distinct words result when the word $aab$ is rotated cyclically, counting identical results only once?
questions.explanation: The distinct rotations are aab, aba, and baa. A cut between identical symbols may repeat a result, but it is counted only once.

questions.prompt: Which statements hold for the reflexive-transitive closure $R^*$ of a relation $R$? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: $R^*$ contains pairs connected by paths of length zero or more.

questions.explanation: The closure preserves R, adds all pairs reachable by paths, and includes the identity relation. Symmetry does not follow.

questions.prompt: Which three properties in the diagram turn a relation into an equivalence relation?

context.content:
flowchart TD
  R["Relation R: check properties"] -->|"reflexive, symmetric, transitive"| E["Equivalence relation"]
  R -->|"reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive"| O["Partial order"]
context.caption: Sets of properties that define two types of relations.

questions.explanation: The diagram associates an equivalence relation with the properties reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.

questions.prompt: On $A=\{1,2,3\}$, let $R=\{(1,2),(2,3),(3,1)\}$. How many self-pairs does $R^+$ contain?
questions.explanation: The cycle $1\to2\to3\to1$ allows each node to return to itself along a path of positive length. Therefore, $R^+$ contains all three self-pairs.

questions.prompt: Which statements about equivalence classes and quotients are correct? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: $A/R$ is the set of all equivalence classes.
An equivalence class $[a]_R$ is a subset of the underlying set.
The quotient counts the same class multiple times for different representatives.
A representative system chooses exactly one element from each class.

questions.explanation: Each class is a subset of A, and A/R collects these classes into a set. Each class appears there only once, even if several elements represent it.

questions.prompt: A reflexive relation does not necessarily partition its underlying set into equivalence classes; symmetry and transitivity must also hold.
questions.explanation: The classes partition the underlying set exactly when the relation is an equivalence relation: reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.
The loop $1\to2\to1$ makes 1 reachable from 1, and the cycle between 1 and 2 also allows $2\to2$. Paths from 1 and 2 continue to 3 and 4; a path from 3 leads to 4. No arrow leaves 4.

questions.prompt: You are building a navigation backend: the relation $R$ stores direct one-way streets. $R^+$ records whether one can travel from $x$ to $y$ using at least one street; $R^*$ also includes a route using zero streets, from every location to itself. Is this correct?
questions.explanation: The transitive closure $R^+$ describes reachability by at least one edge. The reflexive-transitive closure $R^*$ also includes paths of length zero and therefore contains every self-relation.

questions.prompt: You type `dis` into a search box; autocomplete shows words that begin with exactly these letters, such as `diskret` and `display`. Which word relation does this search filter use?

options.text: Infix relation: `dis` occurs contiguously somewhere in the word.
Conjugacy: the word is formed by a cyclic shift.
Suffix relation: `dis` occurs at the end of the word.
Prefix relation: `dis` occurs at the beginning of the word.

questions.explanation: `dis` is a prefix of `diskret` and `display` because it occurs at the beginning of each. An infix could also occur in the middle of a word.

questions.prompt: A four-digit PIN consists of digits from 0 to 9; a leading 0 is allowed. How many different PINs are possible?
questions.explanation: There are 10 possibilities for each of the four positions. Thus, there are $10^4=10\,000$ possible PINs; as words, these are all strings of length 4 over an alphabet of 10 symbols.

questions.prompt: You assign integer user IDs to one of 8 database shards: the shard depends on the remainder when the ID is divided by 8. IDs 26 and 34 therefore end up in the same group. Which relation on the IDs describes exactly this grouping?

options.text: Prefix relation: one ID begins with the digits of the other.
Reachability: one ID leads to the other through several connections.
Divisibility: one ID is an integer multiple of the other.
Congruence modulo 8: same remainder when divided by 8.

questions.explanation: Both 26 and 34 have remainder 2 when divided by 8. Having the same remainder modulo a fixed number is an equivalence relation and groups IDs into equivalence classes.

questions.prompt: Your game uses the symbols {a, b, c}. Repetition is allowed. How many different words of length 4 can you form?
questions.explanation: Each of the four positions has 3 possible symbols. So there are $3^4=81$ words in $\Sigma^4$.

questions.prompt: Let $C$ be a set of contacts. For each contact, a phone number is cleaned by removing only spaces, parentheses, and hyphens; the digits retain their order. Two contacts $c,d\in C$ are equivalent exactly when their cleaned numbers are identical. Which statement always holds?

options.text: The relation is an equivalence relation; its equivalence classes form a partition of $C$.
The relation is symmetric but not transitive.
Two contacts can be equivalent only if their original numbers are identical character by character.
The relation is a strict partial order on phone numbers.

questions.explanation: Equality of the cleaned numbers is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. Therefore, this relation is an equivalence relation; its classes are disjoint and together equal $C$, so they form a partition.

questions.prompt: A weekly planner groups whole-number day indices according to whether they have the same remainder when divided by 12. How many equivalence classes are there?
questions.explanation: The possible remainders are 0 through 11, so there are 12 classes. Two day indices belong to the same class exactly when their difference is a multiple of 12.

questions.prompt: You manage three roles with these permissions: `Lesen` = {read}, `Export` = {read, export}, `Admin` = {admin}. Define $X\,R\,Y$ when the permissions of $X$ are a subset of the permissions of $Y$. What kind of relation is $R$ on these roles?

options.text: A total order in which every pair of roles is comparable.
A strict partial order that contains no self-relations.

questions.explanation: The subset relation is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive, so it is a partial order. `Lesen` and `Admin` are incomparable; therefore, the order is not total.

questions.prompt: A relation on five states is a subset of $A\times A$. What is the maximum number of distinct ordered pairs that $A\times A$ can contain? Self-relations are allowed.
questions.explanation: For each of the 5 possible starting elements, there are 5 possible destinations. Thus, $A\times A$ contains exactly $5\cdot5=25$ pairs; an endorelation can contain all of these pairs at most.

questions.prompt: On a circular game board, the word `abcd` is written. A scanner can start reading at a different position, so it might recognize `cdab`, for example. The order of the letters around the circle is preserved. Which relation connects the two words?

options.text: Prefix relation: one word occurs at the beginning of the other.
Arbitrary permutation: individual letters may be freely rearranged.
Conjugacy: cut the word, then swap the two parts.

questions.explanation: `abcd` can be cut into `ab` and `cd`; swapping the parts produces `cdab`. This is conjugacy: a cyclic shift that preserves the order.
